Servile

SUR-vyle · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Servile is excessively willing to serve or please.

The new waiter's servile flattery -- constant compliments and low bows -- made the other diners visibly uncomfortable.

Worked Example

Employees noticed that the assistant manager grew strangely servile whenever the regional director walked in, laughing at every joke and fetching coffee unasked.

The sudden, excessive eagerness to please someone more powerful -- laughing at every joke, fetching coffee unasked -- is exactly the servile behavior the word describes.

How Servile Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

obsequious

obsequious: excessively eager to please or obey

fawning

fawning: displaying showy flattery

Antonyms

defiant

defiant: boldly resistant to authority

independent

independent: free from outside control or influence

How Strong Is It? — helpful → servile → obsequious

helpful vs. servile

helpful vs. servile: Being helpful just means willing to assist; being servile means being excessively, almost uncomfortably eager to please, often at the cost of self-respect.

obsequious vs. servile

obsequious vs. servile: Obsequious pushes servile even further, adding a note of insincere, calculated flattery aimed specifically at gaining favor.

Sort It Out

Build the Word

The pieces

root — serv

root — serv: slave (Latin (servus))

suffix — -ile

suffix — -ile: pertaining to (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: The root serv- ('slave,' from Latin servus) plus -ile ('pertaining to') gives 'like a slave' -- servile behavior serves and pleases others with no self-respect held back.

Use the root in a new word: serve

Use the root in a new word: serve: Serve shares the same servus root as servile, though servile keeps the negative, excessive edge that plain 'serve' doesn't have.

Root Check

Word Choice

Servile describes a personality trait or manner directed at pleasing people, especially those in power. Compare Slavish (this same unit), which describes blind imitation of ideas or rules rather than eagerness to please a person.
